title: The Psychology of Waiting
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

paragraphs.text: Some years ago, the managers of an airport in Houston, Texas, faced a stream of complaints from passengers about the time they had to wait for their luggage. The managers responded by employing more baggage handlers, and the average wait fell to eight minutes, well within what the industry considers acceptable. The complaints continued. Looking more closely, the managers found that passengers took about one minute to walk from their arrival gate to the baggage hall and then spent seven minutes standing beside the carousel. The solution they adopted was to move the arrival gates further away and to send bags to the most distant carousel. Passengers now walked for six minutes and waited for two. The complaints virtually ceased.

The story, whose details have doubtless been polished in the retelling, illustrates what researchers who study queues have long maintained: the experience of waiting is governed less by its actual length than by how it feels. People are poor judges of time. Surveys in which customers are asked how long they have just waited typically produce figures about a third higher than the true ones. And the feeling of a wait can be altered far more cheaply than the wait itself.

The first principle, set out in an influential 1985 paper by the business scholar David Maister, is that occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time. This is why mirrors are commonly placed beside lifts. In the mid-twentieth century, as tall office buildings multiplied, their managers were troubled by complaints about slow lifts; mirrors gave people something to do – checking their appearance, or discreetly observing others – and the complaints declined, although the lifts were no faster. It is also why supermarkets surround their checkouts with magazines and sweets, an arrangement that has the further advantage of selling them.

A second principle is that uncertain waits feel longer than known ones. A passenger told that a train is delayed by twenty minutes may be annoyed but can settle down to wait; one given no information grows steadily more anxious. Some organisations exploit this by deliberately overstating the wait. Theme parks routinely post waiting times for their rides that are longer than the true ones, so that visitors who reach the front after forty minutes, having been warned to expect fifty, feel they have gained something. The opposite error – a promise that is not kept – produces a disproportionate degree of anger.

Nothing, however, affects people in a queue as powerfully as their sense of fairness. The basic rule of the queue is that those who arrive first are served first, and violations of it are resented even by those who do not lose by them. This explains a curious preference. When several separate lines lead to several counters, as in most supermarkets, the average wait is exactly the same as when a single winding line feeds all the counters, as in many banks and airports. Yet customers consistently say they prefer the single line, and in experiments some have been willing to wait considerably longer in order to have it. In the single line, nobody who arrived later can be served sooner. With separate lines, there is always the galling possibility that the next one will move faster – and people notice the line that is overtaking them far more readily than the one they are overtaking.

Fairness has its limits as a guide to design, all the same. A strict first-come, first-served rule is not always efficient: a hospital emergency department that treated patients purely in order of arrival would let some die. Most people accept priority based on need. They are far less comfortable with priority based on payment, although this is increasingly common. Many theme parks and airports now sell the right to join a shorter line, and the evidence suggests that those left in the ordinary line resent it more when the privileged line is in plain view. Some operators have accordingly taken care to route their paying customers through a separate entrance, out of sight.

Finally, there is the matter of how a wait ends. Psychologists have shown that people's memory of an experience is dominated by its most intense moment and by its conclusion, rather than by its duration. A queue that moves slowly at first and then speeds up is remembered more favourably than one of the same length that does the reverse. The implication for managers is that the last impression matters most – which may be why the Houston passengers, whose bags now appeared almost as soon as they reached the carousel, went home content. It would be easy to dismiss all this as mere manipulation. But if a wait cannot be shortened, there is surely no virtue in leaving it as unpleasant as possible.

items.stem: What did the managers of the Houston airport discover when they examined the problem more closely?

options.A: Passengers spent most of the time standing in one place.
options.B: The baggage handlers were working too slowly.
options.C: The average wait was longer than the industry considers acceptable.
options.D: Passengers had difficulty finding the baggage hall.

items.stem: The writer tells the Houston story in order to show that

options.C: how a wait is experienced matters more than how long it lasts.
options.D: reducing waiting times costs too much.

items.stem: According to the writer, magazines and sweets are displayed near supermarket checkouts

options.A: purely because they sell well there.
options.B: to keep customers occupied and, in addition, to make sales.
options.C: to make the queues look shorter than they are.
options.D: because customers had complained about slow service.

items.stem: Why do theme parks overstate the waiting times for their rides?

options.A: to discourage visitors from joining the longest queues
options.B: because it is impossible to predict the times accurately
options.C: to persuade visitors to pay for access to a shorter line
options.D: so that visitors feel pleased when the wait turns out to be shorter

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
groups.limit:
Write
YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

items.text: The account of events at the Houston airport may not be accurate in every detail.
People generally believe that they have waited for less time than they really have.
On average, customers in a single winding line are served sooner than those in separate lines.
Banks adopted the single-line system before airports did.
Selling access to shorter lines has increased the profits of theme parks.
Efforts to improve the experience of waiting can be justified.

groups.limit: Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.title: What shapes the experience of waiting

rows.text: According to David Maister, time passes more quickly for people who are {37}. A wait also feels shorter when its length is known; a person given no information becomes more and more {38}. The most powerful influence of all, however, is people's sense of {39}. Finally, the way a wait is remembered depends heavily on its most intense moment and on its {40}, not on how long it lasted.

questions.explain:
答案是 A。經理們發現旅客走到行李大廳只要一分鐘，然後 spent seven minutes standing beside the carousel，八分鐘裡有七分鐘是站著等。
陷阱：C 剛好相反，八分鐘是 well within what the industry considers acceptable；B 的問題在增加人手後就已經處理了，抱怨卻沒有停。
questions.quote: then spent seven minutes standing beside the carousel

questions.explain:
答案是 C。第二段直接說這個故事 illustrates：等待的體驗 is governed less by its actual length than by how it feels。
解題關鍵：問「作者為什麼講這個故事」的題目，答案通常在故事結束後的下一句，找 illustrates、shows 這類動詞。
questions.quote: the experience of waiting is governed less by its actual length than by how it feels

questions.explain:
答案是 B。作者把這個做法放在「有事做的時間感覺比較短」這個原則下（It is also why...），又補充它 has the further advantage of selling them。
陷阱：A 的 purely 太絕對，銷售只是 further advantage（額外的好處）；D 的抱怨是電梯的例子，不是超市。
questions.quote: an arrangement that has the further advantage of selling them

questions.explain:
答案是 D。遊客被告知要等五十分鐘，結果四十分鐘就排到，feel they have gained something。
陷阱：C 的付費快速通道在第六段才出現，和高估等候時間無關；A、B 文章都沒有提。
questions.quote: visitors who reach the front after forty minutes, having been warned to expect fifty, feel they have gained something

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。作者說這個故事的 details have doubtless been polished in the retelling（細節在轉述中無疑被修飾過）。
同義轉換：polished in the retelling ＝ may not be accurate in every detail。
questions.quote: The story, whose details have doubtless been polished in the retelling

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。顧客估計的等候時間通常比實際 about a third higher，也就是高估，不是低估。
解題關鍵：higher than the true ones 與題目的 less time 方向相反。
questions.quote: typically produce figures about a third higher than the true ones

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。作者說兩種排法 the average wait is exactly the same。顧客偏好單一隊伍是因為公平，不是因為比較快。
陷阱：顧客的「偏好」容易被誤讀成「比較快」。作者稱它為 a curious preference，正因為平均等待時間並沒有差別。
questions.quote: the average wait is exactly the same as when a single winding line feeds all the counters

questions.explain:
答案是 NOT GIVEN。文章只說單一隊伍常見於 many banks and airports，沒有說哪一種場所先開始採用。
陷阱：banks 寫在 airports 前面只是列舉的順序，不代表時間先後。
questions.quote: as in many banks and airports

questions.explain:
答案是 NOT GIVEN。文章說很多主題樂園和機場販賣排短隊伍的權利，也談到其他人的反感，但沒有提到這是否讓利潤增加。
陷阱：「有在賣」不等於文章說「賺更多」。
questions.quote: Many theme parks and airports now sell the right to join a shorter line

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。最後兩句：這些做法很容易被當成 mere manipulation，But 如果等待無法縮短，there is surely no virtue in leaving it as unpleasant as possible。
解題關鍵：作者的立場在 But 之後。no virtue in leaving it unpleasant 換句話說，就是讓等待好過一點是正當的。
questions.quote: But if a wait cannot be shortened, there is surely no virtue in leaving it as unpleasant as possible.

questions.explain:
答案是 occupied（有事做的）。Maister 的第一個原則是 occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time。
陷阱：不能填 unoccupied，意思相反。feels shorter 對應題目的 passes more quickly。
questions.quote: occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time

questions.explain:
答案是 anxious（焦慮）。沒有得到任何資訊的旅客 grows steadily more anxious。
同義轉換：grows steadily more ＝ becomes more and more。
陷阱：annoyed 是「被告知延誤二十分鐘」的旅客，不是沒得到資訊的那一位。
questions.quote: one given no information grows steadily more anxious

questions.explain:
答案是 fairness（公平）。原文 Nothing, however, affects people in a queue as powerfully as their sense of fairness。
同義轉換：Nothing... as powerfully as ＝ the most powerful influence of all。
questions.quote: Nothing, however, affects people in a queue as powerfully as their sense of fairness.

questions.explain:
答案是 conclusion（結尾）。人對一段經驗的記憶 is dominated by its most intense moment and by its conclusion, rather than by its duration。
陷阱：duration 是被否定的那一個（rather than）。題目已經寫出 most intense moment，另一個因素就是 conclusion。
questions.quote: people's memory of an experience is dominated by its most intense moment and by its conclusion, rather than by its duration
